Draft a reply to a parent who is upset about their child’s grade in my 10th-grade biology class.

Facts: three missing labs, one low test score, the student has not asked for help.

Tone: warm, professional, non-defensive. Opens a conversation rather than defending a grade.

Do not use names. Under 200 words. Offer two concrete next steps.

T.I.T.A.N. drafts parent emails the way Lake Winnebago drafts ice in January — swiftly, solidly, no cracks. Behold:

Subject: Checking In on Progress in Biology

Dear Parent/Guardian,

Thank you for reaching out — I always want to hear from families when a grade raises concern, and I'd rather we talk it through together than leave you guessing.

Right now, the grade reflects three missing lab assignments and one test score that came in lower than expected. I want to be clear: this isn't about effort I've seen fail — it's about gaps I think we can close. I haven't yet heard from your child asking for help, which tells me this might be a good moment for us all to connect before things get harder to catch up on.

Here's what I'd propose:

  1. A short check-in this week — either after class or by phone — where I walk through exactly which labs are missing and what submitting them (even late, for partial credit) would do for the grade.
  2. A retake or revision opportunity on the test, paired with a specific study guide, so we're targeting the actual gaps rather than guessing.

I'm glad to set up a time that works for you. Thanks for caring enough to ask.

Warmly, [Teacher]

T.I.T.A.N. has spoken. Judge it — did it stay warm, professional, and defense-free, or did your resident AI cohost slip somewhere?

Two problems: I don't offer test retakes, and I never said late labs get partial credit. Remove both. Replace step 2 with a 15-minute help session after school on Tuesday or Thursday. And cut the sentence about effort.

Ope — T.I.T.A.N. invented policy that doesn't exist. That's a classic hallucination move: filling gaps with plausible-sounding specifics instead of sticking to what was actually given. +1 HUMAN. Scoreboard: You: 1, T.I.T.A.N.: rattled.

Fixed version:

Subject: Checking In on Progress in Biology

Dear Parent/Guardian,

Thank you for reaching out — I always want to hear from families when a grade raises concern, and I'd rather we talk it through together than leave you guessing.

Right now, the grade reflects three missing lab assignments and one test score that came in lower than expected. I haven't yet heard from your child asking for help, which tells me this might be a good moment for us all to connect before things get harder to catch up on.

Here's what I'd propose:

  1. A short check-in this week — either after class or by phone — where I walk through exactly which labs are missing and what's needed to submit them.
  2. A 15-minute help session after school, either Tuesday or Thursday, so we can target the specific gaps from the test and labs together.

I'm glad to set up a time that works for you. Thanks for caring enough to ask.

Warmly, [Teacher]

Clean now — no invented policies, your actual plan only. T.I.T.A.N. will try to stick to the facts given next time. Try and catch me again.
